On 11/7/11 4:52 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> The email was about the bugs rats example, which I checked in (what I
> think is) a working version of. JAGS kills us on speed, but that's
> only because it's a really easy problem and JAGS can therefore get
> nearly independent samples every iteration.

I always say that benchmarking isn't easy to
make "objective".

I was expecting this sort of speed lag for simple
examples. In fact, I brought it up with Andrew when he
was asking about BUGS/JAGS vs. Stan comparisons and with
Matt when we were talking about Stan vs. RM-HMC.

We should look better on scalability in terms of
amount of data, complexity and size of parameters,
and number of samples. Judging from the lag at
the end of sampling, I think JAGS (like BUGS) buffers all
the samples in memory, but then maybe that's just an
R interface issue (which we'll probably inherit because
R's not scalable).

What I'd like to see is intrinsic model complexity on
the horizontal axis (e.g., number of predictors, data
size, etc.) versus resource usage on the vertical axis
(e.g., time or memory to get to a given ESS), with
lines for JAGS, NUTS (straight C++ implementation and
auto-dif implementation) and RM-HMC.

I think we'll look better than JAGS on more complex models
and at larger scale. And we should look better than
RM-HMC at larger-scale models.

If it's only a compile time lag, we could work on that.

If it's something deeper, I also wrote into the proposal
that we'd build Gibbs with compilation. That should run
faster than BUGS or JAGS (less compilation time).

> I just tried to write an email to stan-dev and was told I don't have
> permission. Could someone look into that?

Daniel's working on it. I hope you're at least getting these
e-mails.

- Bob

messages.subject: return value for distributions outside of support?
parts:
Daniel's working on error propagation for the
libs and we're now wondering what to do for
distributions given arguments outside their
support?

Sensible options seem to be either to

1. return 0 (or -infinity on the log scale), or

2. throw an exception

If we throw an exception, we'll probably want to make
it a special one so that someone could catch it
and go on, for instance by rejecting a sample.

Some of the more serious libs, like Boost, allow
you to configure error handling at a global level to
do one or the other, but I'd rather just go with one
for simplicity.

As Daniel brought up, in our case, it's almost
always going to be the result of either (a) some
arithmetic precision error, or (b) a model
specification error. We can try to control (a) by
the same trick Matt applied to log1p(), namely
bounding returns in the expected range.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Rats coding in Stan
parts:
I have a couple of comments on the Rats example.

0. Looking at a real example, I'm not sure putting
the derived parameters up front helps. Opinions?

1. We're not doing ourselves any favors on these
examples by using deviation as the parameter for
the normal distribution as we wind up taking sqrt()
all over the place.

It'd be interesting to see how slight changes to
non-conjugate priors would affect the comparison.


2. As Daniel pointed out, you can replace:

for (i in 1:N)
for (j in 1:T)
mu[i,j] <- alpha[i] + beta[i]*(x[j] - xbar);

and

for (i in 1:N)
for (j in 1:T)
Y[i,j] ~ normal(mu[i,j], sigma_c);

with

for (i in 1:N)
for (j in 1:T)
Y[i,j] ~ normal(alpha[i] + beta[i]*(x[j] - xbar), sigma_c);

As is, the

double mu[N,T];

declaration will get compiled to a variable

std::vector<std::vector> mu;

and the mu[i,j] accessor compiled to mu[i][j].
There's a whole lot of push_back going on to
build it all.

Matt -- is mu[i] going to return a reference
to the embedded item? If it's copying, it's
a real problem.


3. We can replace their (x[j] - xbar) with
a new defined data item x_centered[j] = x[j] - xbar.
And we could compute xbar inside the program if it's
really just the average value of the x. That's what the
"derived data" block's meant to expedite.


4. I'd like to move to the convention where our loops look like:

for (n in 1:N)
for (t in 1:T)
y[n,t] ~ ...

Also, the use of sigma_c and alpha_c and beta_c is just crazy.
At least if they're going to do this, then

alpha[i] ~ normal(alpha_c, alpha_sigma);

should be

alpha[i] ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);

for consistency.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: benchmarking NUTS vs. JAGS vs. RM-HMC
parts:
I'm glad to see that NUTS can still kick
HMC's ass!

I checked in a revised version of the Rats
model following the conventions I laid out
(and also following Andrew's desire to have
deviation be the parameter, not variance).
And also the BDA/ARM conventions of not trying to
capitalize (or boldface) random variables,
matrices, or anything other than true constants.
For Andrew's edification, I've appended the model below.

I verified Matt's time report of about 11s for
the revised model in Stan/NUTS (g++ -O3). This was after
removing the vector<vector> allocation and
inlining it into the distribution.

JAGS is about 100 times faster here,
getting 3500 samples in a tenth the time it
takes us to get around 350, and that's not even
counting model compilation time. Ouch.

Then again, we may want to be a bit easier on ourselves by
not throwing away the initial half of the samples
in a case like this that's likely to converge quickly.
At least when we're doing performance comparisons.
That might get the time closer to a factor of 50 :-)

I'll have to ask Matt about profiling when we're both in
the office -- I want to see where the time's
going now. It could be largely in auto-dif, but
I wouldn't think it'd be an overall factor of 50.

Using g++ -O3 takes about 12s -- in line with what
you're reporting. So I don't think the std::vector
accesses were the issue.

- Bob

# http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/Vol1.pdf
# Page 3: Rats
data {
int(0,) N;
int(0,) T;
double x[T];
double xbar;
double y[N,T];
}
parameters {
double alpha[N];
double beta[N];
double mu_alpha;
double mu_beta;
double(0,) sigma_y;
double(0,) sigma_alpha;
double(0,) sigma_beta;
}
derived parameters {
double(0,) sigmasq_y;
double(0,) sigmasq_alpha;
double(0,) sigmasq_beta;

sigmasq_y <- sigma_y * sigma_y;
sigmasq_alpha <- sigma_alpha * sigma_alpha;
sigmasq_beta <- sigma_beta * sigma_beta;
}
model {
mu_alpha ~ normal(0, 100);
mu_beta ~ normal(0, 100);
sigmasq_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
sigmasq_alpha ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
sigmasq_beta ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
for (n in 1:N) {
alpha[n] ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);
beta[n] ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);

y[n,t] ~ normal(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar), sigma_y);
}
}

For formal evaluations, I think we should weight examples by how long
they take. The difference between waiting one second and 10 seconds is
small compared with the amount of time needed to edit a text file.

I think random-walk Metropolis would do substantially worse than
NUTS/HMC, since Langevin (i.e. HMC with 1 step) does terribly. The
"problem" is that Gibbs is actually really fast for this model. (If
only we had this problem for all models!) Since the amount of work
needed for one well implemented Gibbs step is comparable to the amount
of work needed for one likelihood evaluation for this model, it's hard
to imagine anything doing much better than Gibbs.

Ordinarily I'd say exception, but I'm not 100% sure. The advantage to

correct, I'm pretty sure), whereas an exception may lead to users
giving up. Maybe we could print out a warning?

from coming up to the extent that's possible.

Matt

> distributions given arguments outside their

>
> Sensible options seem to be either to
>
> 1.  return 0 (or -infinity on the log scale), or
>
> 2.  throw an exception
>
> If we throw an exception, we'll probably want to make
> it a special one so that someone could catch it
> and go on, for instance by rejecting a sample.
>

parts:
If Gibbs is fast in this example, I don't see why Metrop wouldn't be fast too. The goal here would not be to beat Gibbs but rather to not be 50 times as slow!

In any case, i agree there's no need to obsess over models that are already fast. The real issue will come when we fit big hierarchical models. If these are slow with Stan, we'll have to do more thinking. And at that point it might help to have developed some intuition from the easy problems.

Finally, 1 sec vs 10 sec is no big deal, but 1 sec vs 50 sec is starting to make a difference. 50 seconds can be a long time to wait, if we're fitting models over and over again.

I hope I summarized enough of the context -- I didn't have
the stamina to interleave all these comments.

0. A factor of 7 for auto-diff vs. direct seems pretty
good to me given that we're doing allocation and managing
the stack. It should get faster when we override the probability
distros in two ways. First, we'll save memory and speed by partially
evaluating results (fewer chainables on the stack holding fewer refs
with fewer steps in derivatives). Second, we won't have to do the
extra calcs for the fixed normal(0,100) mean and deviation
parameters (though that's pretty small in this case). In fact,
this reminds me that we should treat centered distros separately, as
they remove a lot of the inner arithmetic -- (x - 0) * (x - 0)
is way worse in auto-dif terms than x * x.

We could approach hand-written speed, I think, if
we did code generation rather than templated taping.
Maybe that's what Paul Hovland at DoE was talking to
Andrew about -- it's what their tools ADIFOR and ADIC
do for Fortran. It's much much harder to do for C++ than for
Fortran or even C, and requires yet another code-gen/compilation
step.

1. Matt -- that's nice analysis of Gibbs vs. Metropolis vs.
Langevin vs. HMC vs. NUTS. It should go in a textbook
somewhere!

What would be nice would be to see a setup where all
the distros are conjugate, but it's still slow w. Gibbs.

What do you mean that Gibbs is scale-invariant? That it
doesn't matter what scale the params are on because you're
doing proper conditional probs? Won't it matter in practice
if you use something like a step-out slice sampler?

And isn't the problem that the scale varies by parameter?
And isn't Riemann-manifold HMC just an attempt to automatically
calc the scale?

2. Now that I think about it, mu[i] has to be a reference,
because it can be on the LHS of an assignment.

3. I brought up the loop issue in case someone thought we
should stick closer to the way the BUGS models were coded.
I'd like to use them as examples of how to code models in
Stan. As Daniel suggested, we should supply a "translation
manual" for helping BUGS users get started. Doing it by
BUGS examples is ideal, so we'll kill two birds with one stone.

4. As to exceptions vs. 0/inf for out-of-support arguments,
you could always catch the exception inside of Stan's HMC
loop and treat it as a complete 0 probability step. It'd
probably even be more efficient than continuing even given
the cost of dispatching exceptions.

Do some of these distributions have well-defined behavior
in the limit of parameters going to 0 or inf? If so, we
could always just implement that behavior. That'd be in
keeping with IEEE math.

We can't just print something, as that's hugely time
consuming and hard to control. That's what JAGS does and it
takes ages for the megabytes of warning messages to print out.
Even if there's a log4j-like package for C++, that's
still costly compared to function evals. We could have a
DEBUG mode controlled at compile time, but that's a huge
pain for users.

There's really no way we can prevent overflows.
A user can just multiply in a loop.

5. In UI reaction time, there's a big jump from
a few milliseconds to the half-second or so when it
becomes really apparent an operation's not "instantaneous".
At that point, if you go beyond a few seconds, users will
check their e-mail, and if you go beyond a minute or two,
they'll find something else to do.

- Bob

Code generation would definitely make things faster (and much more
memory efficient, I think). It's tricky in general, but I suspect not
as hard for the average-case Stan model, which will usually just be a
sum of predefined functions of (possibly transformed) model variables.
Something to think about, especially because the memory cost of taping
poses real limitations on model size.

In this example, there's a surprising amount of overhead associated
with repeatedly computing log(sigma). It's not huge, and it'd probably
be a pain to eliminate, but we should add that sort of thing to the
list of sources of suboptimal efficiency.

BTW, on os x the "Time Profiler" in the Instruments application is a
really nice profiler. I think it's meant to replace Shark, which is
what I used to use. That's how I got alerted to the log(sigma)
business.

By "Gibbs is scale-invariant," I meant in the case where you've got
analytic conditionals for everything. It's a little less
scale-invariant when slice sampling using the doubling method, and
much less if you're using the stepping-out method. RMHMC does address
the issue of different parameters having different scales, but it goes
much further and (effectively) rotates the space so that the
parameters are locally uncorrelated. If you're dealing with a
multivariate normal target distribution, it basically tries to turn it
into a standard isotropic normal.

I think most distributions have sort of well defined behavior for
extreme parameter values—normals turn into deltas or improper uniforms
as sigma goes to 0 or inf, t's turn into normals or deltas as nu goes
to inf or 0, gammas turn into deltas as shape goes to 0 or rate goes
to inf, etc. IEEE math won't necessarily make these things happen like
they should by default. There's a little bit of a performance hit for
enforcing correct behavior, but it's probably pretty minor in c++
compared with evaluating logs and exps.

Matt

> Code generation would definitely make things faster (and much more

We'd still have to have all the intermediate variables
and adjoints built up as variables only now they'd be
allocated on the program stack instead of our own stack.

For instance, with (a*b), we push a vari onto the stack
holding the value of (a*b) and the partial of this expression
w.r.t. the root expression (which gets instantiated in
the backward pass). We'd need both these as local variables
on the execution stack with code generation. We also
store the pointers to a and to b on the vari object. Those
would instead be linked inside the code itself, which would
almost certainly be more efficient in time (in space?) than
managing the derivative propagation stack and memory management
ourselves.

With optimization, the compiler could almost certainly optimize
our generated code to get rid of things that aren't used.
But most variables are used if they're auto-dif variables;
if they're constants, we don't put them on the stack either.
